title: The Emergency, 1975-77

cards.b: For 21 months, from 25 June 1975 to 21 March 1977, India lived under a national Emergency. Civil liberties were suspended, the press was censored and the opposition jailed. The episode shapes how we think about executive power, judicial independence and constitutional safeguards.

The ground was 'internal disturbance'. Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha ruled in State of UP v Raj Narain that Indira Gandhi's Rae Bareli win was invalid for electoral malpractice. The Supreme Court gave a conditional stay on 24 June.

• Fundamental rights suspended (Art. 359); MISA used for detention; about 1 lakh arrested.
  • Press censorship; newspapers like the Indian Express protested.
  • The 42nd Amendment (1976) added 'socialist, secular, integrity', Fundamental Duties, curbed judicial review, and extended Lok Sabha's term to six years.
  • Sanjay Gandhi's five-point programme: forced sterilisation and slum clearances (Turkman Gate).
  • Twenty-point programme of Indira Gandhi.

The Supreme Court, 4:1, held that during the Emergency a detained person could not move a High Court for habeas corpus, since the right to life and liberty (Art. 21) was suspended. Justice H.R. Khanna dissented, saying life and liberty cannot be taken away without the authority of law, and he was superseded as CJI. In Puttaswamy (2017) the Court declared ADM Jabalpur wrongly decided.

Indira Gandhi called elections in March 1977. The Janata Party (JP's push) won about 295 seats, Congress about 154; Indira and Sanjay lost their seats. Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress PM. The Shah Commission (1977-78) inquired into excesses, finding abuse of power, and the Janata government passed the corrective amendments.

Safeguards added: 'internal disturbance' replaced by 'armed rebellion'; the Cabinet's written advice to the President is needed; the Emergency must be approved by special majority within one month and renewed every six months; Arts. 20 and 21 cannot be suspended; Lok Sabha can vote to revoke it by simple majority; the right to property was removed from Part III (to Art. 300A); Lok Sabha term reduced to five years again.

Defence: law and order was collapsing, the Emergency was constitutional, and it brought discipline. Critique: personal motive, centralisation, 'committed judiciary' and bureaucracy. Scholars: Granville Austin's Working a Democratic Constitution (1999) calls it a test and a lesson. Related debate on 'authoritarian democracy' and the party's internal decay. In 2024 the Government declared 25 June as Samvidhan Hatya Diwas.

• Constitutional safeguards need active citizens, press and courts.
  • Judicial independence is fragile (supersession of judges in 1973 and 1977).
  • Basic structure survived: Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975) and Minerva Mills (1980) limited the 39th and 42nd Amendments.
  • Opposition unity after JP changed the party system.

The 1977 mandate became the model for 'anti-incumbency' voting; the lesson reappears in debates about preventive detention (NSA, UAPA), internet shutdowns, and press freedom. Questions often ask you to compare the Emergency with Art. 356 or with 2020s concerns about democratic backsliding.
